answer:
Based on my comprehensive search of NBA draft data from 2015-2024, here are the drafted players born in the first week of August (August 1-7) who scored more than 15 points per game in at least one NBA season:

## Confirmed Players

### 1. Kristaps Porziņģis
- **Birth Date:** August 2, 1995
- **Draft Year:** 2015 (4th overall pick, New York Knicks)
- **Scoring Milestone:** Averaged **22.7 PPG** in the 2016-17 season (All-Star caliber performance)
- Additional seasons with 15+ PPG: 22.3, 23.8, career average ~19.5 PPG

### 2. Anthony Edwards
- **Birth Date:** August 5, 2001
- **Draft Year:** 2020 (1st overall pick, Minnesota Timberwolves)
- **Scoring Milestone:** Averaged **25.9 PPG** in the 2023-24 season, **27.6 PPG** in 2024-25 season, **28.8 PPG** in 2025-26 season
- Multiple seasons exceeding 15+ PPG consistently throughout his career

---

These are the only two players I could definitively confirm meet all three criteria:
1. Drafted between 2015-2024 drafts
2. Born between August 1-7 (first week of August)
3. Scored 15+ PPG in at least one regular season

Note: Many highly regarded scorers from this era (like Ja Morant, Tyrese Haliburton, Scottie Barnes, etc.) do not qualify because they were born outside the first week of August.

## 1.outline
A Canadian basketball player, his team is the Oklahoma City Thunder of the NBA , and his main position is point guard . The most commonly used abbreviation is SGA, and in Korea, it is called Suga, which is based on the abbreviated name.[[7]](https://en.namu.wiki/w/%EC%85%B0%EC%9D%B4%20%EA%B8%B8%EC%A0%80%EC%8A%A4%EC%95%8C%EB%A0%89%EC%82%B0%EB%8D%94#fn-7)
Immediately after being selected by the Charlotte Hornets in the 2018 NBA Draft , he was traded and made his debut with the Los Angeles Clippers . After his first season, he was traded again to the Oklahoma City Thunder in exchange for Paul George . Subsequently, with OKC, he won the scoring title, MVP, championship, and Finals MVP all at once during the 24-25 season.

## 1.outline
A Canadian basketball player, his team is the Oklahoma City Thunder of the NBA , and his main position is point guard . The most commonly used abbreviation is SGA, and in Korea, it is called Suga, which is based on the abbreviated name.[[7]](https://en.namu.wiki/w/%EC%85%B0%EC%9D%B4%20%EA%B8%B8%EC%A0%80%EC%8A%A4%EC%95%8C%EB%A0%89%EC%82%B0%EB%8D%94#fn-7)
Immediately after being selected by the Charlotte Hornets in the 2018 NBA Draft , he was traded and made his debut with the Los Angeles Clippers . After his first season, he was traded again to the Oklahoma City Thunder in exchange for Paul George . Subsequently, with OKC, he won the scoring title, MVP, championship, and Finals MVP all at once during the 24-25 season.

# NBA birthdays: Players born on August 2
With a player born on each day, our birthday series continues with the NBA players born on August 2.
Joel Bartilotta, Rotowire.com
September 24, 2025 3:17 PM
Kristaps Porziņģis is among the players born on August 2.
With over 5,000 players in NBA history, at least one player was born on every day of the calendar year – including four leap day ballers. Our day-by-day breakdown of the players born on each day of the year continues.
Below are the most notable NBA players born on August 2.
* * *

# NBA birthdays: Players born on August 2
### Kristaps**Porziņģis (1995)**
Porziņģis helped put Latvia on the map as a basketball country when he was selected fourth overall in the 2015 NBA Draft by the New York Knicks. “Zinger” finished second in Rookie of the Year voting in his debut campaign, showcasing one of the most unique skillsets from any seven-footer in NBA history. Not only was Porziņģis an elite shot-blocker, he proved to be one of the most dangerous shooters as well. That rookie season was just a taste, with Porziņģismaking an All-Star appearance just two years later. He averaged 22.7 points, 6.6 rebounds, 1.2 assists and 2.4 blocks in that breakout campaign.
It was his final season in NY before spending the next three years with the Dallas Mavericks. Porziņģis then spent two seasons with the Washington Wizards starting in 2021, averaging a career-high 23.2 points, 8.4 rebounds, 2.7 assists and 1.5 blocks in 2023. He then went on to be a key part of Boston’s 2024 NBA Championship. As of 2025, Porziņģis is starting his next chapter as a member of the Hawks.

# NBA birthdays: Players born on August 2
### Cedric Ceballos (1969)
Caballos had a unique NBA journey, playing for five teams throughout his 11-year career. He was selected 48th overall in the 1990 NBA Draft out of Cal State Fullerton by the Phoenix Suns. After limited playing time through his first two seasons, Ceballos broke out in 1993. He led the league in field goal percentage (58 percent) that year out of the forward position, paving the way to becoming a starter the following year. That was his final season in Phoenix before having a career year with the Los Angeles Lakers the following season.
Ceballos averaged a career-high 21.7 points, 8.0 rebounds, 1.8 assists and 1.0 steals while making his first All-Star appearance and finishing 15th in MVP voting. He played three years in LA and then rejoined the Suns in 1996. Ceballos closed his career with stints in Dallas, Detroit and Miami before officially retiring in 2001. He also finished third in Sixth Man of the Year voting with the Mavs in 2000 and took down the Slam Dunk Contest in 1992.

# NBA birthdays: Players born on August 2
### Kristaps**Porziņģis (1995)**
Porziņģis helped put Latvia on the map as a basketball country when he was selected fourth overall in the 2015 NBA Draft by the New York Knicks. “Zinger” finished second in Rookie of the Year voting in his debut campaign, showcasing one of the most unique skillsets from any seven-footer in NBA history. Not only was Porziņģis an elite shot-blocker, he proved to be one of the most dangerous shooters as well. That rookie season was just a taste, with Porziņģismaking an All-Star appearance just two years later. He averaged 22.7 points, 6.6 rebounds, 1.2 assists and 2.4 blocks in that breakout campaign.
It was his final season in NY before spending the next three years with the Dallas Mavericks. Porziņģis then spent two seasons with the Washington Wizards starting in 2021, averaging a career-high 23.2 points, 8.4 rebounds, 2.7 assists and 1.5 blocks in 2023. He then went on to be a key part of Boston’s 2024 NBA Championship. As of 2025, Porziņģis is starting his next chapter as a member of the Hawks.

# NBA birthdays: Players born on August 2
### Cedric Ceballos (1969)
Caballos had a unique NBA journey, playing for five teams throughout his 11-year career. He was selected 48th overall in the 1990 NBA Draft out of Cal State Fullerton by the Phoenix Suns. After limited playing time through his first two seasons, Ceballos broke out in 1993. He led the league in field goal percentage (58 percent) that year out of the forward position, paving the way to becoming a starter the following year. That was his final season in Phoenix before having a career year with the Los Angeles Lakers the following season.
Ceballos averaged a career-high 21.7 points, 8.0 rebounds, 1.8 assists and 1.0 steals while making his first All-Star appearance and finishing 15th in MVP voting. He played three years in LA and then rejoined the Suns in 1996. Ceballos closed his career with stints in Dallas, Detroit and Miami before officially retiring in 2001. He also finished third in Sixth Man of the Year voting with the Mavs in 2000 and took down the Slam Dunk Contest in 1992.

#### Kentucky, Freshman

A raw forward with the requisite athletic traits to be a go-to scorer if he puts it all together.
**Shades Of:** Tobias Harris, Al Harrington, Jeff Green

### KEVIN KNOX
#### Kentucky, Freshman
###### PLUSES
*   Skilled finisher around the rim; uses either hand, can yam on defenders, and has fluid body control driving around opponents.  
*   Displays pick-and-roll scoring upside; can pull up, get to the rim, or take advantage of smaller players on a switch.  
*   Flashes shooting skills spotting up and running off screens, though his percentages are mediocre.  
*   Savvy scorer without the ball; shows a knack for spacing on the perimeter and when to cut. Runs the floor hard in transition.  
*   Potentially versatile defender if he locks in — he has the athleticism, length, and lateral quickness.

### KEVIN KNOX
#### Kentucky, Freshman
###### MINUSES
*   Settles for too many midrange jumpers and floaters early in the shot clock.  
*   Lacks passing instincts.  
*   Average rebounder; teams will be hurting on the boards if they choose to play Knox as a 4 in smaller lineups.  
*   Takes too many naps on defense, fails to contest shots, keeps his hands by his side, and rarely makes high-impact or timely plays.  
*   Versatility is theoretical; he’s not quick enough to contain elite guards and needs to get a lot stronger to defend interior bigs.

A prototypical 3-and-D prospect who has made steady progress over his three college seasons and may have untapped upside.
**Shades Of:** Robert Covington, Eddie Jones, Tony Snell

### MIKAL BRIDGES
#### Villanova, Junior
###### PLUSES
*   Unselfish team player who keeps the ball moving and plays within himself.  
*   Competitive, experienced defender who has the speed to contain guards and length to handle wings.  
*   Effective catch-and-shooter with NBA range; flashes the body control necessary to develop into a shooter off screens.  
*   Attacks with purpose as a straight-line driver; he reads the floor well and can finish at the rim with either hand or with power.  
*   Capable of beating mismatches on the low post.  
*   Flashes playmaking potential as a passer off the dribble. If his handle improves, he could be a pick-and-roll threat.

### MIKAL BRIDGES
#### Villanova, Junior
###### MINUSES
*   Lanky upper and lower body may put a cap on his defensive versatility -- can he defend larger forwards?  
*   Lacks crafty ball-handling moves and is a subpar shooter off the bounce.  
*   Has improved every year in college as a shooter, but may struggle in the NBA due to the hitch in his shot.  
*   Doesn’t consistently show a star mentality; vanishes occasionally, despite playing a central role for Villanova.

#### Alabama, Freshman

A fearless score-first point guard who needs to learn how to control his intensity.
**Shades Of:** Eric Bledsoe, Patrick Beverley, Marcus Banks

### COLLIN SEXTON
#### Alabama, Freshman
###### PLUSES
*   He’s here to kick ass and chew bubblegum—and that attitude is contagious.  
*   He’s a potential lockdown defender against guards due to his lateral quickness, length, and effort.  
*   Stays engaged off-ball fighting through screens; he’s always a threat to intercept passes.  
*   Shifty ball handler with a quick first step; he gets where he wants on the floor using a litany of advanced moves.  
*   Ambidextrous and aggressive finisher at the rim. He would have better percentages in that zone if his shot selection improved.  
*   Draws a ton of fouls and shoots well from the line.  
*   Possesses a relaxed jumper off both the catch and dribble, with NBA range.  
*   Showcases toughness in adverse situations. He once scored 40 points to keep Alabama in a game while playing 3-on-5.

### COLLIN SEXTON
#### Alabama, Freshman
###### MINUSES
*   Forces low-quality shots against rim protection and hoists jumpers early in the clock, rather than making plays for teammates.  
*   Lacks pure passing skills; he forces high-risk passes or low-quality shots at a frustrating rate.  
*   He can hone his passing ability by improving his accuracy and the velocity he puts on passes.  
*   He’ll need to prove he can play a more controlled brand of play within a system.  
*   He’s lanky, and will need to get stronger without losing quickness to maximize his defensive potential.

A raw forward with the requisite athletic traits to be a go-to scorer if he puts it all together.
**Shades Of:** Tobias Harris, Al Harrington, Jeff Green

### KEVIN KNOX
#### Kentucky, Freshman
###### PLUSES
*   Skilled finisher around the rim; uses either hand, can yam on defenders, and has fluid body control driving around opponents.  
*   Displays pick-and-roll scoring upside; can pull up, get to the rim, or take advantage of smaller players on a switch.  
*   Flashes shooting skills spotting up and running off screens, though his percentages are mediocre.  
*   Savvy scorer without the ball; shows a knack for spacing on the perimeter and when to cut. Runs the floor hard in transition.  
*   Potentially versatile defender if he locks in — he has the athleticism, length, and lateral quickness.

### KEVIN KNOX
#### Kentucky, Freshman
###### MINUSES
*   Settles for too many midrange jumpers and floaters early in the shot clock.  
*   Lacks passing instincts.  
*   Average rebounder; teams will be hurting on the boards if they choose to play Knox as a 4 in smaller lineups.  
*   Takes too many naps on defense, fails to contest shots, keeps his hands by his side, and rarely makes high-impact or timely plays.  
*   Versatility is theoretical; he’s not quick enough to contain elite guards and needs to get a lot stronger to defend interior bigs.

Title: R. J. Hunter
Chunks: 4,5,6,7,8,9,10,11,12,21,22,23,24
Many know Hunter from seeing highlights of his clutch buzzer-beater in the second round of the 2015 NCAA tournament, but hitting a shot like that was nothing new for him. In his sophomore year, Hunter scored a career-high 41 points against [UTSA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTSA_Roadrunners_men's_basketball "UTSA Roadrunners men's basketball"), making a school single-game-record 12 three-pointers. The 12 threes were also the most in the country during the year and set a new Sun Belt Conference record. In another game that year, he hit the game-winning shot with 11.1 seconds to play against Arkansas State. Another clutch shot came in a game in which Hunter scored 31 points including a crucial 3-pointer with seven seconds left at [UT Arlington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UT_Arlington_Mavericks_men's_basketball "UT Arlington Mavericks men's basketball") to send the game to overtime.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-GSU_Player_Bio-1)
Hunter was named [Sun Belt Conference Basketball Player of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_Belt_Conference_Men's_Basketball_Player_of_the_Year "Sun Belt Conference Men's Basketball Player of the Year") as well as the Sun Belt Conference Male Athlete of the Year.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-SUNBELT-2) He was also named the Men's Georgia College Player of the Year by the Atlanta Tipoff Club.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-3)

In his final season at GSU, Hunter averaged a career-high 19.7 points, scoring a school-record season total of 688 points (a school record he broke each season). He also averaged 4.7 rebounds and 3.6 assists per game. In addition, he made 202 free-throws (No. 7 in the NCAA that year), second-most in school history, while swiping 75 steals, third-most in a single season in program history. The most noteworthy record he set was total career points. Midway through just his third season, Hunter overtook Rodney Hamilton's record of 1,515 points with a basket in front of a GSU home crowd against [UL Lafayette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana_Ragin'_Cajuns_men's_basketball "Louisiana Ragin' Cajuns men's basketball") on January 24, 2015. Hunter finished the year with a career total of 1,819 points.

The Panthers finished the 2014–15 season as the Sun Belt Conference regular season and tournament champions. With their Sun Belt Tournament championship win over [Georgia Southern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_Southern_Eagles_men's_basketball "Georgia Southern Eagles men's basketball"), the Panthers received a bid to the [NCAA tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_NCAA_Division_I_men's_basketball_tournament "2015 NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament"). In the round of 64, No. 14 seed Georgia State trailed the No. 3 seed Baylor by 12 points with just 2:53 to play. Hunter took over and scored 12 of the Panthers' final 13 points, including a 30-foot 3-pointer with 2.6 seconds remaining to secure their electrifying come-from-behind upset win, which caused his coach (and father) Ron to fall off his stool in jubilation. The moment was selected as No. 2 in the NCAA's top 10 moments of the tournament, was included in the "One Shining Moment" montage following the championship game,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-GSU_Player_Bio-1)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-dagger-4) and was one of three nominees for the 2015 Best Upset ESPY Award.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-ESPYS-5)
Hunter was again named both Sun Belt Conference Basketball Player of the Year and the Sun Belt Conference Male Athlete of the Year.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-SUNBELT-2) R.J. was also the only player from a school in Georgia to be named to the Naismith Trophy watch list that season.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-6)

*   All-time Georgia State University leader in points (1,819)  
*   All-time Georgia State University leader in free throws made (448), in free-throw percentage (.853), and in consecutive free throws made (38)  
*   All-time Georgia State University leader in 3-pointers made (253)  
*   Single-season Georgia State University leader in 3-pointers made (100, 2013–14)  
*   Single-season Georgia State University leader free-throw percentage (.882, 2013–14)  
*   Single-game Sun Belt Conference leader in 3-pointers made (12)  
*   Single-game Sun Belt Conference leader in free-throw percentage (1.000 16–16, 2015)

## Professional career
[edit]

## Professional career
### Boston Celtics (2015–2016)
[edit]
On June 25, 2015, Hunter was selected with the 28th overall pick in the 2015 NBA draft by the Boston Celtics.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-7) On July 27, he signed his rookie-scale contract with the Celtics.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-8) After averaging just 2.8 points per game over his first eight NBA games, Hunter scored 12 points on 5-of-6 shooting off the bench against the Atlanta Hawks on November 24.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-9) During his rookie season, Hunter received multiple assignments to the Maine Red Claws, the Celtics' Development League affiliate.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-10) On October 24, 2016, Hunter was waived by the Celtics.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-11)

## Professional career
### Chicago Bulls (2016)
[edit]
On October 27, 2016, Hunter signed with the Chicago Bulls.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-12) He was waived by the Bulls on December 29, 2016, after appearing in three games.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-13) During his time with Chicago, he had multiple assignments to the Windy City Bulls of the NBA Development League.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-14)

## Professional career
### Long Island Nets (2017)
[edit]
On January 6, 2017, Hunter was acquired by the Long Island Nets of the NBA G-League.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-15) Four days later, he made his debut for Long Island in a 120–112 loss to the Fort Wayne Mad Ants, recording 22 points, three assists and two steals in 25 minutes off the bench.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-16)

## Professional career
### Rio Grande Valley Vipers (2017–2018)
[edit]
After failing to find a team to participate in training camp under the preseason, he would be assigned to the Rio Grande Valley Vipers of the D-League on October 24, 2017. Hunter made his debut with the team on November 4.

Another clutch shot came in a game in which Hunter scored 31 points including a crucial 3-pointer with seven seconds left at [UT Arlington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UT_Arlington_Mavericks_men's_basketball "UT Arlington Mavericks men's basketball") to send the game to overtime.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-GSU_Player_Bio-1)
Hunter was named [Sun Belt Conference Basketball Player of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_Belt_Conference_Men's_Basketball_Player_of_the_Year "Sun Belt Conference Men's Basketball Player of the Year") as well as the Sun Belt Conference Male Athlete of the Year.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-SUNBELT-2) He was also named the Men's Georgia College Player of the Year by the Atlanta Tipoff Club.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-3)
texts.5: In his final season at GSU, Hunter averaged a career-high 19.7 points, scoring a school-record season total of 688 points (a school record he broke each season). He also averaged 4.7 rebounds and 3.6 assists per game. In addition, he made 202 free-throws (No. 7 in the NCAA that year), second-most in school history, while swiping 75 steals, third-most in a single season in program history. The most noteworthy record he set was total career points. Midway through just his third season, Hunter overtook Rodney Hamilton's record of 1,515 points with a basket in front of a GSU home crowd against [UL Lafayette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana_Ragin'_Cajuns_men's_basketball "Louisiana Ragin' Cajuns men's basketball") on January 24, 2015. Hunter finished the year with a career total of 1,819 points.
texts.6:
The Panthers finished the 2014–15 season as the Sun Belt Conference regular season and tournament champions. With their Sun Belt Tournament championship win over [Georgia Southern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_Southern_Eagles_men's_basketball "Georgia Southern Eagles men's basketball"), the Panthers received a bid to the [NCAA tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_NCAA_Division_I_men's_basketball_tournament "2015 NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament"). In the round of 64, No. 14 seed Georgia State trailed the No. 3 seed Baylor by 12 points with just 2:53 to play. Hunter took over and scored 12 of the Panthers' final 13 points, including a 30-foot 3-pointer with 2.6 seconds remaining to secure their electrifying come-from-behind upset win, which caused his coach (and father) Ron to fall off his stool in jubilation. The moment was selected as No. 2 in the NCAA's top 10 moments of the tournament, was included in the "One Shining Moment" montage following the championship game,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-GSU_Player_Bio-1)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-dagger-4) and was one of three nominees for the 2015 Best Upset ESPY Award.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-ESPYS-5)
Hunter was again named both Sun Belt Conference Basketball Player of the Year and the Sun Belt Conference Male Athlete of the Year.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-SUNBELT-2) R.J. was also the only player from a school in Georgia to be named to the Naismith Trophy watch list that season.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-6)

texts.9:
## Professional career
### Boston Celtics (2015–2016)
[edit]
On June 25, 2015, Hunter was selected with the 28th overall pick in the 2015 NBA draft by the Boston Celtics.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-7) On July 27, he signed his rookie-scale contract with the Celtics.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-8) After averaging just 2.8 points per game over his first eight NBA games, Hunter scored 12 points on 5-of-6 shooting off the bench against the Atlanta Hawks on November 24.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-9) During his rookie season, Hunter received multiple assignments to the Maine Red Claws, the Celtics' Development League affiliate.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-10) On October 24, 2016, Hunter was waived by the Celtics.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-11)
texts.10:
## Professional career
### Chicago Bulls (2016)
[edit]
On October 27, 2016, Hunter signed with the Chicago Bulls.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-12) He was waived by the Bulls on December 29, 2016, after appearing in three games.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-13) During his time with Chicago, he had multiple assignments to the Windy City Bulls of the NBA Development League.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-14)
texts.11:
## Professional career
### Long Island Nets (2017)
[edit]
On January 6, 2017, Hunter was acquired by the Long Island Nets of the NBA G-League.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-15) Four days later, he made his debut for Long Island in a 120–112 loss to the Fort Wayne Mad Ants, recording 22 points, three assists and two steals in 25 minutes off the bench.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-16)
texts.12:
## Professional career
### Rio Grande Valley Vipers (2017–2018)
[edit]
After failing to find a team to participate in training camp under the preseason, he would be assigned to the Rio Grande Valley Vipers of the D-League on October 24, 2017. Hunter made his debut with the team on November 4.

The 12 threes were also the most in the country during the year and set a new Sun Belt Conference record. In another game that year, he hit the game-winning shot with 11.1 seconds to play against Arkansas State. Another clutch shot came in a game in which Hunter scored 31 points including a crucial 3-pointer with seven seconds left at [UT Arlington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UT_Arlington_Mavericks_men's_basketball "UT Arlington Mavericks men's basketball") to send the game to overtime.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-GSU_Player_Bio-1)
Hunter was named [Sun Belt Conference Basketball Player of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_Belt_Conference_Men's_Basketball_Player_of_the_Year "Sun Belt Conference Men's Basketball Player of the Year") as well as the Sun Belt Conference Male Athlete of the Year.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-SUNBELT-2) He was also named the Men's Georgia College Player of the Year by the Atlanta Tipoff Club.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-3)

In his final season at GSU, Hunter averaged a career-high 19.7 points, scoring a school-record season total of 688 points (a school record he broke each season). He also averaged 4.7 rebounds and 3.6 assists per game. In addition, he made 202 free-throws (No. 7 in the NCAA that year), second-most in school history, while swiping 75 steals, third-most in a single season in program history. The most noteworthy record he set was total career points. Midway through just his third season, Hunter overtook Rodney Hamilton's record of 1,515 points with a basket in front of a GSU home crowd against [UL Lafayette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana_Ragin'_Cajuns_men's_basketball "Louisiana Ragin' Cajuns men's basketball") on January 24, 2015. Hunter finished the year with a career total of 1,819 points.

The Panthers finished the 2014–15 season as the Sun Belt Conference regular season and tournament champions. With their Sun Belt Tournament championship win over [Georgia Southern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_Southern_Eagles_men's_basketball "Georgia Southern Eagles men's basketball"), the Panthers received a bid to the [NCAA tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_NCAA_Division_I_men's_basketball_tournament "2015 NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament"). In the round of 64, No. 14 seed Georgia State trailed the No. 3 seed Baylor by 12 points with just 2:53 to play. Hunter took over and scored 12 of the Panthers' final 13 points, including a 30-foot 3-pointer with 2.6 seconds remaining to secure their electrifying come-from-behind upset win, which caused his coach (and father) Ron to fall off his stool in jubilation. The moment was selected as No. 2 in the NCAA's top 10 moments of the tournament, was included in the "One Shining Moment" montage following the championship game,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-GSU_Player_Bio-1)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-dagger-4) and was one of three nominees for the 2015 Best Upset ESPY Award.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-ESPYS-5)
Hunter was again named both Sun Belt Conference Basketball Player of the Year and the Sun Belt Conference Male Athlete of the Year.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-SUNBELT-2) R.J. was also the only player from a school in Georgia to be named to the Naismith Trophy watch list that season.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-6)

## Professional career
### Boston Celtics (2015–2016)
[edit]
On June 25, 2015, Hunter was selected with the 28th overall pick in the 2015 NBA draft by the Boston Celtics.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-7) On July 27, he signed his rookie-scale contract with the Celtics.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-8) After averaging just 2.8 points per game over his first eight NBA games, Hunter scored 12 points on 5-of-6 shooting off the bench against the Atlanta Hawks on November 24.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-9) During his rookie season, Hunter received multiple assignments to the Maine Red Claws, the Celtics' Development League affiliate.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-10) On October 24, 2016, Hunter was waived by the Celtics.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-11)

## Professional career
### Chicago Bulls (2016)
[edit]
On October 27, 2016, Hunter signed with the Chicago Bulls.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-12) He was waived by the Bulls on December 29, 2016, after appearing in three games.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-13) During his time with Chicago, he had multiple assignments to the Windy City Bulls of the NBA Development League.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-14)

## Professional career
### Long Island Nets (2017)
[edit]
On January 6, 2017, Hunter was acquired by the Long Island Nets of the NBA G-League.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-15) Four days later, he made his debut for Long Island in a 120–112 loss to the Fort Wayne Mad Ants, recording 22 points, three assists and two steals in 25 minutes off the bench.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hunter#cite_note-16)

## Professional career
### Rio Grande Valley Vipers (2017–2018)
[edit]
After failing to find a team to participate in training camp under the preseason, he would be assigned to the Rio Grande Valley Vipers of the D-League on October 24, 2017. Hunter made his debut with the team on November 4.
